## The shape of the bug (WI-6512)

```rust
fn cmdline_looks_like_serve(cmdline: &str) -> bool {
    let lower = cmdline.to_ascii_lowercase();
    lower.contains("serve.mjs") || lower.contains("serve.ts")
}
```

`discovery_pid_alive(pid)` = *the pid exists* **AND** *its cmdline passes the
predicate above*. It was written (WI-3282) to stop a stale `operator.json` pid
from false-**positively** matching after the OS recycled it onto an unrelated
process. Reasonable goal, and the recycled-pid risk is real — this box wraps
pids roughly daily under fleet load.

The defect is which process it names. `serve.mjs` / `serve.ts` is the
**supervisor**: it owns embedded-PG startup and migrations, and then runs the
actual HTTP/IPC host, `hono-host`. **The host is the process that writes
`~/.papercusp/endpoint-ipc*.json` and owns the IPC socket.** The check was
asking about the wrong process.

Measured on the dev box, 2026-07-28 — every operator that had published a live
advertisement, versus the predicate:

| advertisement | real `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` | matches? |
|---|---|---|
| `endpoint-ipc.3070.json` (release) | `node …/papercup-release/apps/operator/dist-host/hono-host.mjs` | **no** |
| `endpoint-ipc.3170.json` (staging) | `node dist-host/hono-host.mjs` | **no** |
| `endpoint-ipc.3270.json` (dev) | `node --require tsx/dist/preflight.cjs --import tsx/dist/loader.mjs bin/hono-host.ts` | **no** |
| …6 further dev instances | same tsx-wrapped form | **no** |

**9 of 9.** Not a sampling artifact — the predicate could not match any operator
this repo actually runs.

## Why it stayed invisible for so long

Two properties combined, and neither is specific to this codebase.

**1. The failure direction was a false NEGATIVE, and a false negative reads as
ordinary absence.** `discovery_pid_alive` returning `false` is
indistinguishable, at every call site, from "the operator genuinely isn't
running yet" — which is a completely normal state during boot. There is no
error to log because, as far as the code is concerned, nothing went wrong.

**2. There was a working fallback underneath.** When IPC could not resolve a
socket, `/api` quietly fell back to the webview's native HTTP transport. That
works. It is merely *slow*, because WebKitGTK/libsoup allows ~6 connections per
host and five long-lived SSE streams eat five of them, leaving one socket for
everything else. Same URL: **9 ms via curl, 2542 ms in-webview.** The owner
experienced this as "clicking an agent in the agents-running dropdown takes
several seconds", and reported it as a database problem. The database was
answering in 75 ms.

A silent false-negative plus a degraded-but-functional fallback is the recipe
for a defect that survives months of use. The system never says it is broken;
it just quietly stops being fast.

## The trigger that turned it fatal

The name check existed for a while without touching IPC. On 2026-07-27,
EI-18763945004822208 fixed a genuine, separately-measured bug — after an
operator restart the discovery file briefly still names the previous, dead pid,
and dialing it produced a resolvable-but-ENOENT connect on *every* `/api` call
(160/160 failed invokes). The fix validated the advertisement before dialing,
and reused `discovery_pid_alive` to do it.

That is how a latent naming bug became a total transport outage: the validation
was correct in intent and its liveness oracle was already wrong. Afterwards
`socket_source` returned `None` on every attempt, so the Rust
`IpcClientHandle` never dialed — including the on-demand re-dial its own doc
comment promised.

> **Reusing an existing predicate imports its bugs into a new blast radius.**
> Before wiring an existing check into a path where a wrong answer is
> catastrophic, verify it against live data from *that* path — not against the
> path it was written for.

## The fix, and why it is split in two

The two questions have opposite failure costs, so they are now two functions:

- **`discovery_pid_exists(pid)`** — name-free, `/proc/<pid>` (or `kill -0`).
  Cannot false-negative on a live process. **This is what the endpoint-ipc
  advertisement path uses.** It still fully preserves the restart-orphan fix
  above, because that failure mode was a pid that no longer *exists*. A recycled
  pid now slips through, and that is deliberate: the cost is one cheap failed
  connect, which `IpcClientHandle::live` reports precisely and retries — versus
  a silent, permanent loss of the transport.
- **`cmdline_looks_like_operator(cmdline)`** — the recycled-pid defense, kept
  for the respawn/reap call sites where a false positive is the expensive
  direction. Now recognizes `hono-host` as well as `serve`.

The general rule:

> **Never gate a transport on a hardcoded entrypoint-name list.** The name rots
> the moment the entrypoint is renamed, rebuilt under a different filename, or
> wrapped by a loader (`tsx` puts the real entrypoint *last* in argv, behind
> `--require`/`--import` flags — a matcher anchored on `argv[1]` would miss it
> too). Where you can, let the operation itself be the oracle: **the dial is the
> authority.** A unix-socket connect is sub-millisecond and answers definitively
> what no amount of process introspection can guess.

## What made it findable

The instrumentation, not the reasoning. Two prior sessions theorised about port
selection and JS retry loops and got nowhere, because the resolver returned a
bare `Option<PathBuf>` — it computed a precise reason and then threw it away at
exactly the moment it mattered.

`socket_source` now returns a `SocketResolution { path, detail }`, and the first
line of the first instrumented run said it outright:

```
[endpoint_ipc] not dialing: selected port 3070: per-port advertises
/home/…/sockets/110896.sock for pid 110896, which is not running (restart
orphan) at /home/…/endpoint-ipc.3070.json; singleton advertises …
```

Pid 110896 was, at that moment, alive and serving. The contradiction between
that line and `kill -0` was the whole diagnosis, and it took seconds.

There is now also `endpoint_ipc_status` (a Tauri command, `withGlobalTauri` so
`window.__TAURI__.core.invoke('endpoint_ipc_status')` works from devtools or
`tauri-agent-tools eval`). It reports the live resolution, the connection state,
and dial/invoke counters, and it deliberately takes no `.await` and uses
`try_lock` — so a `client: "dial-in-flight"` that persists across polls *is* the
diagnosis of a hung dial, rather than a diagnostic that hangs alongside it.

> **If a resolver can fail, make it return the reason, not just the absence.**
> `Option<T>` is the wrong return type for anything whose `None` a human will
> later have to explain. The reason is free at the point of computation and
> expensive to reconstruct anywhere else — here it was being reconstructed by
> hand from `ss`, `/proc`, and JSON files, once per investigation.

### Side-lesson: a new Tauri command needs a capability entry, and nothing but a live invoke will tell you

`endpoint_ipc_status` compiled, registered in `collect_commands!`, and appeared
67 times in the running binary — and still failed at runtime with
`endpoint_ipc_status not allowed. Command not found`. Tauri v2 gates app
commands through `src-tauri/capabilities/default.json`; the command needs an
`allow-<command-name-in-kebab-case>` entry beside its siblings:

```json
"allow-endpoint-invoke",
"allow-endpoint-cancel",
"allow-endpoint-ipc-status",
```

`cargo check`, `cargo test`, and the whole Rust suite pass without it. The only
thing that catches it is invoking the command from a live webview. If you add a
Tauri command, add the capability entry in the same edit, and prove it with one
real `invoke` — the error text says "Command not found", which sends you
hunting through registration code that is already correct.

## Recurrence guards

- `cmdline_check_accepts_the_real_operator_entrypoints` pins the **verbatim**
  cmdlines captured from live operators. Rename the entrypoint and this test
  fails loudly, instead of the transport dying quietly.
- `cmdline_check_still_rejects_an_unrelated_node_process` keeps the widened
  matcher from degrading into "anything with node in it".
- `advertisement_gate_accepts_a_live_pid_whose_cmdline_is_unrecognized` pins the
  design decision itself: a live pid is never vetoed for having a cmdline we
  failed to anticipate. It asserts the precondition (the test binary really does
  not look like an operator) so it cannot pass for the wrong reason.
